title: Fuse double-variable operands into addsd/subsd/mulsd/divsd memory operands (addsd xmm, [rax])
description: compile_elist_sse2 already fuses a CCONST that directly precedes add/sub/mul/div into a RIP-relative memory operand (has_pending_mem_operand, lines 3816-3820, 3895-3921, 3928-3983), but a CVAR in the same position is always materialized with 'mov rax, imm64; movsd xmm[d], [rax]' followed by a reg-reg arithmetic op. Since the variable's address is already in RAX (RAX cache, 3805-3814), the load can be folded into the arithmetic instruction itself: emit 'addsd xmm[d-1], [rax]' (F2 0F 58 /r with ModRM rm=rax) instead of 'movsd xmm[d],[rax]; addsd xmm[d-1],xmm[d]'. Restrict to M64FP variables, keep the existing dup-peephole (3824-3836) checked first so 'x x mul' still uses the register dup, and extend the pending-operand state to distinguish rip-const vs rax-mem. The arithmetic is identical (same load value, same op, same rounding) so results are bit-identical. Because normalize_commutative_operands (2929-2978) puts the larger subtree first, single-leaf variables land in the fusable second-operand slot very frequently. Optional follow-up (NOT bit-identical, so fast_math-only or skip): teach is_sse2_compatible (3248-3267) not to count fused operands as a stack push, which would keep borderline-deep expressions on SSE2 instead of falling back to x87.
location: C:/plms/bsd_licensed/mexce/mexce.h lines 3816-3820 (pending-operand state), 3839-3848 (CVAR load path to extend), 3895-3921 and 3928-3983 (existing CCONST fusion to mirror), 3248-3267 (optional compat-check awareness)
affected_expressions: All SSE2 expressions with bound double variables as the second operand of +, -, *, / — i.e. the majority of plain arithmetic expressions (x+y, x*y+z, polynomial terms).
expected_impact: Removes one 4-byte movsd instruction and one µop per fused operand, and frees one XMM stack slot. Probe: 'x*y+z' body shrinks from 13 to 11 instructions (~15% fewer). Realistic 2-5% avg eval improvement on arithmetic-dense expressions given ~6ns/eval; also smaller code (icache) and reduced register pressure for libm spill paths.
evidence: Verified by reading compile_elist_sse2 (mexce.h 3795-4116) and by byte dump: 'x+y' emits 48 B8 <&y> F2 0F 10 08 F2 0F 58 C1 (mov rax; movsd xmm1,[rax]; addsd xmm0,xmm1) where F2 0F 58 00 (addsd xmm0,[rax]) suffices. The constant case already proves the fusion pattern works in this codebase ('2*x' style fusion at 3908-3913).

verdict.reasoning: Verified against mexce.h on master. (1) Not implemented: the CVAR path in compile_elist_sse2 (lines 3839-3848) always emits movsd xmm[depth],[rax] (emit_sse2_load_from_rax, line 3361) followed by reg-reg addsd/subsd/mulsd/divsd (lines 3938/3952/3966/3980); only CCONST gets memory-operand fusion, via RIP-relative placeholders (has_pending_mem_operand at 3816-3820, set at 3908-3913, consumed at 3929-3976). No [rax]-memory-operand arithmetic exists in the SSE2 backend. (2) Correctness: addsd/subsd/mulsd/divsd xmm, m64 performs the identical 64-bit load and identical double-precision-rounded operation as movsd+reg-reg, so results are bit-identical (NaN, -0.0, Inf, denormals included); scalar mem operands have no alignment requirement; no fast_math gating needed for the main idea. The fusion window is exactly one elist element (CVAR immediately followed by the add/sub/mul/div CFUNC), so RAX cannot be clobbered in between, and the dup-peephole invariant (prev leaf materialized in xmm[depth-1]) survives because a fused leaf is always followed by a CFUNC, never another leaf. The depth>0 guard from the constant path (line 3901) must be mirrored, and fusion must be restricted to M64FP (M32FP needs cvtss2sd, integers need x87 conversion) — the proposal scopes both correctly. Encoding is trivially derived from existing helpers (emit_sse2_addsd_rip_placeholder at 3479, just ModRM rm=000 with no disp32); the proposal's byte dump for 'x+y' is accurate. (3) The claim that single-leaf variables frequently land in the fusable second-operand slot is confirmed: normalize_commutative_operands (2929-2978) splices the larger chunk first for add/mul. (4) One sub-claim refuted: 'frees one XMM stack slot / reduced register pressure for libm spill paths' is overstated — fused operands are consumed by the immediately following op and are never live across a libm call, so the XMM save count in emit_sse2_libm_unary_call (based on depth at call time) is unchanged; only transient peak depth drops, which matters only for the optional is_sse2_compatible follow-up (itself correctly flagged as non-bit-identical since it shifts expressions from x87 80-bit to SSE2). The optional follow-up should probably be skipped rather than fast_math-gated. Tried to refute the core idea and failed: it is unimplemented, semantically exact, cheap to implement, and strictly reduces instruction count on a very common pattern.
verdict.impact_assessment: Real but modest. Saves one 4-byte movsd and one fused-domain uop per fused variable operand; applies to most plain arithmetic expressions (x+y, x*y+z, polynomial terms), which dominate a benchmark averaging ~6ns/eval. However, the load-to-op dependency-chain latency is unchanged — the win is frontend bandwidth and code size only — and tiny expression bodies are largely latency/call-overhead bound. Expect roughly 1-3% average eval improvement on the full 44229-expression benchmark (the proposal's 2-5% is plausible only for arithmetic-dense subsets), plus a genuine code-size reduction. Detectable with the existing median round-robin timing, but this is a low-single-digit micro-optimization, not a step change. Compile-time cost is negligible (slightly fewer bytes emitted); implementation risk is low.

title: Use movaps instead of movsd for XMM register-to-register moves (kills false dependencies, enables move elimination)
description: emit_sse2_mov_reg_reg (3379-3396) emits 'movsd xmm[dst], xmm[src]' (F2 0F 10 /r). The reg-reg form of movsd merges into the destination's upper 64 bits, creating a false dependency on the destination register's previous value, and is not eligible for zero-latency move elimination on Intel (SNB+) or AMD (Zen+) cores. Replacing the opcode with movaps (0F 28 /r, same ModRM/REX scheme) copies all 128 bits: it is 1 byte shorter, has no false dependency, and is move-eliminated at rename (0 cycles, no execution port). The upper 64 bits of the simulated-stack registers are never observed anywhere in the backend (all ops are scalar; the return value is the low qword of xmm0), so results are bit-identical. This single helper is used by the leaf-dup peephole (3829, e.g. x*x), all libm argument/result marshalling (3714, 3724, 3758-3768, 3777-3778), and the final result move to xmm0 (4113). The same one-line change automatically fixes the post-call 'movsd xmm[arg],xmm0' result moves where a false dep chains into freshly returned libm values.
location: C:/plms/bsd_licensed/mexce/mexce.h lines 3379-3396 (emit_sse2_mov_reg_reg); call sites 3829, 3714, 3724, 3758-3778, 4113
affected_expressions: Expressions with repeated leaves (x*x), all libm transcendental calls (sin/cos/tan/exp/log*/logb), and any expression whose result ends above xmm0.
expected_impact: Small but universal and free: ~1 byte smaller per move, removes 1-cycle+false-dep moves from dependency chains; likely <1-2% avg, slightly more on transcendental-marshalling-heavy expressions. Zero downside.
evidence: Byte dumps confirm movsd reg-reg today: 'x*x' emits F2 0F 10 C8 (movsd xmm1,xmm0) before mulsd; 'sin(x)+sin(y)+sin(z)' emits F2 0F 10 C1 / F2 0F 10 C8 around each call rax. Intel/AMD optimization guidance explicitly recommends movaps over movsd for reg-reg copies (partial-register merge + no move elimination for movsd).

verdict.reasoning: Tried to refute and failed. (1) Not implemented: emit_sse2_mov_reg_reg at mexce.h:3379-3396 emits F2 [REX] 0F 10 /r (merging reg-reg movsd); no movaps appears anywhere in the file. The cited evidence dump is accurate (dst=1,src=0 -> F2 0F 10 C8). (2) Technically correct and bit-identical without fast_math: I enumerated every XMM consumer in the SSE2 backend — addsd/subsd/mulsd/divsd (+RIP-fused forms), sqrtsd, roundsd, movsd stores (stack spill at 3604, CSE store at 4091), xorpd/andpd mask ops (3988-4010), libm calls, and the return in xmm0's low qword. None observe XMM upper 64 bits architecturally; the bitwise mask ops touch uppers but raise no FP exceptions and their upper results are never consumed; Win64/SysV ABIs ignore upper bits of scalar double args. No comisd/cvt/shuffle/horizontal ops exist in this backend (grep confirmed). NaN/-0.0/Inf are copied bit-exactly. Reg-reg movaps never faults (alignment irrelevant), and the proposed encoding ([REX] 0F 28 /r with REX.R=dst, REX.B=src, F2 prefix dropped since movaps is an NP opcode) is correct and 1 byte shorter. (3) Microarch claims check out: merging movsd reg-reg has a true dependency on prior dst and is not move-eliminated; movaps is eliminated on IVB+/Zen+ and never worse on older x64 cores — this is what gcc/clang/MSVC themselves emit for double reg-reg copies. (4) No hidden costs: one-line change, code shrinks, compile time unchanged, x87 backend and 32-bit builds untouched (helper is a no-op without MEXCE_64). The only weakness is magnitude, addressed in impact_assessment.
verdict.impact_assessment: Real but small. The helper fires only on: (a) the adjacent-identical-leaf dup peephole (line 3829, e.g. x*x), where the merging movsd creates a loop-carried dependency through dst's upper 64 bits across benchmark iterations — eliminating it could give a few percent on those specific expressions; (b) libm marshalling moves, but only when depth>1 (plain sin(x) at depth 1 emits zero moves since arg_reg==0), and there the libm call cost dominates so the gain is sub-1%; (c) the final move at 4113, which is essentially dead since well-formed expressions end at depth 1. Expressions using pow or comparisons fall back to x87 entirely (3252-3257) and are unaffected. Averaged over the 44229-expression suite at ~6ns avg eval, expect well under 1% — likely 0.1-0.5%, possibly near measurement noise even with median round-robin timing. However, it is strictly free: smaller code (1 byte/move), zero correctness risk, zero compile-time cost, never slower on any x64 core. Worth doing as a trivial hygiene fix; do not expect a headline benchmark win.

title: [fast_math] Lower pow with constant integer (and ±0.5) exponents in the SSE2 backend instead of forcing whole-expression x87 fallback
description: Any expression containing '^' currently runs on the x87 backend: the SSE2 pre-check (m_sse2_simplify_mode, 5656-5664) runs before optimizers and is_sse2_supported_function (3185-3214) does not include 'pow', and pow_optimizer (2249-2371) always packages the power as a pre-compiled x87 blob with debug_desc set, which is_sse2_compatible rejects at 3252. Even 'x^2' compiles to x87 (verified), while the semantically identical 'x*x' compiles to SSE2. Additionally, when asmd_optimizer in SSE2-simplify mode merges x*x*x into a pow node (4478-4482), the post-optimization compat check fails and the entire expression is re-parsed from scratch with x87 forced (5838-5850), paying double compile cost. Proposal: (a) accept pow(chunk, CCONST n) in the pre-check when n is ±0.5 or a small integer; (b) skip pow_optimizer's x87-blob conversion for these nodes in sse2-simplify mode (keep its nested-power folding at 2216-2246); (c) in compile_elist_sse2, lower n=2 to 'mulsd xmm[d-1],xmm[d-1]', n=0.5 to sqrtsd, and |n|<=k to a square-and-multiply mulsd sequence using one scratch register (mirroring emit_integer_power_sequence, 2165-2209), with -n adding a 1.0/x divsd. This also fixes a separate inefficiency: the current abs_factor==2 SSE2 path duplicates the whole term chunk in the elist (4470-4476), re-evaluating multi-node bases twice; a single-eval 'sq' lowering computes the base once. Gating: moving these expressions from x87 (53-bit precision with extended exponent range on Windows, 64-bit on Linux) to SSE2 changes results in exponent-range/precision edge cases, so this must sit behind the existing fast_math option per the bit-identity rule.
location: C:/plms/bsd_licensed/mexce/mexce.h lines 3185-3214 and 3230-3277 (compat checks), 2249-2338 (pow_optimizer x87 blob), 4470-4482 (asmd SSE2 pow/x^2 emission), 5656-5664 and 5838-5850 (pre-check and fallback re-parse), 2165-2209 (square-and-multiply model)
affected_expressions: All expressions containing '^' or pow() with constant exponents, and products that asmd merges into powers >= 3 (x*x*x...). Likely a large fraction of the 44229-expression benchmark.
expected_impact: Moves a whole expression class from the x87 backend (~7ns+) to SSE2 (~6ns): 10-20% eval improvement for power-containing arithmetic expressions, plus eliminates the full set_expression re-parse (compile-time) when asmd creates pow nodes, and eliminates double evaluation of non-leaf squared bases.
evidence: Probe confirms: 'x^2' -> backend=x87 (bytes DD 00 DC C8 + fstp/movsd epilogue) while 'x*x' -> backend=sse2; '(x+y)^2' and 'x^2+y^2' also x87. Code: 'pow' absent from supported sets (3189-3206); pow_optimizer sets debug_desc (2327) which is_sse2_compatible rejects (3252); fallback re-parse at 5843-5850; chunk duplication for ^2 at 4472-4475.

(1) Not implemented: 'pow' is absent from is_sse2_direct_function/is_sse2_libm_function (mexce.h:3189-3206; comment at 3196-3198 explicitly says pow is excluded), so the SSE2 pre-check (5659) fails for any '^' expression; pow_optimizer (2249-2371) unconditionally packages constant-exponent powers as x87 blobs with debug_desc set (2327), which is_sse2_compatible rejects (3252). (2) Probe independently confirmed (compiled with MinGW g++, get_backend()): 'x*x' -> sse2 but 'x^2', 'x^3', 'x^0.5', '(x+y)^2', 'x^2+y^2', and notably 'x*x*x' all -> x87. The 'x*x*x' case confirms the asmd-merge path (4478-4482 emits a pow node in sse2-simplify mode) triggering the full set_expression re-parse with x87 forced (5843-5850), i.e., double compile cost. (3) Scoping is correct: moving from x87 (53-bit precision with extended intermediate exponent range on Windows, 64-bit precision on Linux) to SSE2 mulsd/sqrtsd chains changes bits in range/precision edge cases, so fast_math gating is the right conservative choice; the proposed lowerings otherwise match existing mexce x87 semantics (fsqrt for ^0.5 incl. sqrt(-x)=NaN, same square-and-multiply tree as emit_integer_power_sequence 2165-2209, x^0->1 incl. NaN base, fdivr for negative exponents). Hidden costs found: (a) the pre-check runs before constant elimination (5659 vs 5786), so exponents written as expressions ('a^2^3', 'a^(2.2*3.3)') are not CCONST at check time and would still fall back to x87 unless extra folding is added; (b) the square-and-multiply lowering needs a scratch XMM register that the depth model in is_sse2_compatible (3245-3273) must account for — Windows allows only 6 XMM registers (3179), so this is a real clobber hazard if unhandled; (c) restructuring pow_optimizer while preserving the nested-power folding and m_power_terms machinery (2216-2246, benchmark-semantics-sensitive) carries regression risk, consistent with the proposer's own 'large effort / medium risk'. I tried to refute the core mechanism and failed — the inefficiency is real, unimplemented, and the fix is technically sound. However, the affected-class size claim is grossly overstated (see impact).
verdict.impact_assessment: Real but tiny on the headline benchmark. Only 170/44229 expressions (0.38%) contain '^', zero contain pow(), and zero match v*v*v triple-product patterns. Of the 170, ~46 have variable exponents (unhelped), and the ~124 numeric-exponent ones include non-integer exponents (generic pow path, unhelped), constant bases (fully const-folded, no eval), and expression-form exponents not yet CCONST at pre-check time. The genuinely helped class is ~0.2% of the benchmark. Per-expression eval gains of 15-25% are plausible (x87 avg 8.0ns vs SSE2 6.0ns per README, plus x87's fstp/movsd epilogue overhead dominates tiny expressions like x^2), giving a benchmark-average improvement of roughly 0.03-0.06% — and only in the SSE2+fast-math config, since fast_math gating leaves the default SSE2 headline number untouched. The compile-time double-parse elimination benefits zero benchmark expressions (no x*x*x patterns; '^' expressions fail the pre-check so no fallback occurs for them). The 'affected_expressions: likely a large fraction of the benchmark' claim is off by ~two orders of magnitude. Value is real for power-heavy real-world workloads (polynomials), but for the stated benchmark this is a niche win that does not justify 'large' effort on benchmark-improvement grounds alone.

title: Load neg/abs sign masks RIP-relatively from the constant pool instead of mov rax,imm64 + xorpd/andpd [rax]
description: neg and abs in compile_elist_sse2 (3984-4011) emit a 10-byte 'mov rax, imm64' pointing at the static sse2_masks (807-818) followed by 'xorpd/andpd xmm,[rax]' (14 bytes total), and the mask address evicts the RAX address cache so a subsequent reload of a previously cached variable address re-emits another 10-byte mov. Extend the existing RIP-relative constant pool (PendingRipConstant + finalize_rip_constants, 3281-3345) to support 16-byte-aligned 16-byte entries and emit 'xorpd xmm, [rip+disp32]' (66 0F 57 05 disp32, 8-9 bytes). Legacy-SSE xorpd/andpd memory operands require 16-byte alignment, so the pool finalizer must pad to 16 for these entries (it currently only 8-aligns doubles, 3315-3318). Results are bit-identical (same mask, same op); RAX and its cache remain untouched, so interleaved variable loads keep their cached address.

affected_expressions: Expressions with unary minus or abs() on the SSE2 backend (neg nodes are also synthesized by asmd_optimizer for negative leading factors, line 4447).
expected_impact: Saves ~6 bytes and one mov per neg/abs, and preserves the RAX variable-address cache across them. Small (<1% avg), mainly code-size/front-end; cheap and aligned with the existing pool infrastructure.
evidence: Byte dump of '-x*y' ends with 48 B8 <&sign_mask> 66 0F 57 00 (mov rax, imm64; xorpd xmm0,[rax]). finalize_rip_constants currently handles only 8-byte doubles with 8-byte alignment (3315-3329), so masks cannot be pooled today.

verdict.reasoning: I tried to refute this and failed on correctness; every cited fact checks out. (1) Not implemented: mexce.h:3985-4011 emits neg/abs via emit_load_rax_if_needed((void*)masks.sign_mask/abs_mask) followed by inline 'xorpd/andpd xmm,[rax]' (66 [REX] 0F 57/54 ModRM), i.e. 10-byte mov rax,imm64 + 4-5 byte op on first use; the RIP constant pool (PendingRipConstant/finalize_rip_constants, 3281-3345) handles only 8-byte doubles with 8-byte NOP padding (3315-3318) and a std::map<double,size_t> dedupe, so 16-byte masks cannot be pooled today. (2) The RAX-eviction claim is real: the cache lambda (3809-3814) is shared between variable addresses (3846/3852/3864) and mask addresses (3988/4002), so a neg/abs between two uses of the same variable forces a second 10-byte address mov. (3) Technically correct: xorpd/andpd with the identical 128-bit mask via [rip+disp32] is bit-identical (no NaN/-0.0/Inf issues; upper-lane XOR is identical in both forms); legacy-SSE m128 operands do require 16-byte alignment, and that is satisfiable because get_executable_buffer (414-422) uses VirtualAlloc/mmap (page-aligned) with the code memcpy'd at offset 0 (5926), so in-buffer padding to 16 gives runtime alignment — the proposal correctly identifies this requirement. Encoding sizes (8 bytes, 9 with REX.R for xmm8-15) are right. Scoped to MEXCE_64 SSE2 only; x87 untouched. (4) Hidden costs are minor but real: the pool dedupe map must be extended (masks are not doubles); total buffer size actually GROWS for typical single-neg expressions (instruction stream shrinks ~6 bytes but the pool gains 16 data bytes + up to 15 padding bytes per expression, whereas the masks currently live once in shared static memory); and repeated same-mask ops cost 8-9 bytes RIP-relative vs 4-5 bytes with the warm RAX cache. None of these invalidate the idea, but the 'code-size saving' framing only holds for the executed instruction stream, not the total allocation.
verdict.impact_assessment: Real but tiny — essentially unmeasurable on the benchmark average. Of the 44229 expressions, only 41 contain abs( and 53 have unary minus on a non-constant operand (constant-only negs are eliminated by the constant-folding pass; asmd_optimizer-synthesized negs at 4447 require a net-negative leading additive factor, which is rare), so roughly 0.2-0.3% of the corpus is affected. Per affected expression the change removes one or two 10-byte mov rax instructions that sit off the xmm dependency chain — a front-end/decode saving only, plausibly 0-2% of a ~4-6ns eval, well below the noise floor that PR #110's median round-robin timing was built to suppress. Aggregate benchmark effect on avg eval time: on the order of 0.001% or less. Worth doing only as cheap code hygiene aligned with the existing pool infrastructure, not as a performance win.

title: Replace the x87 fild/fstp/movsd round-trip for integer variables with cvtsi2sd (and break the cvtss2sd false dependency)
description: Integer-typed bound variables in the SSE2 backend go through a 3-instruction x87 detour with a store-forwarding memory round-trip: fild [rax]; fstp qword [rsp]; movsd xmm[d],[rsp] (3861-3881). Replace with direct conversions: M32INT -> 'cvtsi2sd xmm, dword [rax]' (F2 0F 2A /r), M64INT -> REX.W form, M16INT -> 'movsx ecx, word [rax]' + 'cvtsi2sd xmm, ecx' (RCX is volatile and unused by the backend). Bit-identical: fild is exact (64-bit significand covers all int64) and fstp m64 rounds once to nearest, exactly like cvtsi2sd's single rounding under default rounding mode. Prepend 'xorps xmm,xmm' to break cvtsi2sd's partial-register false dependency on whatever the caller left in that register; the same xorps treatment applies to the float-variable cvtss2sd path (3850-3859), which currently merges into uninitialized upper bits and inherits a false dep on caller state. Side benefit: this removes the only non-libm use of the [rsp] scratch slot, which unblocks dropping the prologue entirely (see separate idea).

affected_expressions: Expressions with bound int16/int32/int64 variables (and, for the dep-break, float32 variables) on the SSE2 backend. No effect on double-only workloads like the main benchmark.
expected_impact: Replaces ~12-15 cycles of x87+store-forward latency and 3 instructions with one ~6-cycle cvtsi2sd (+1 zeroing idiom); int-variable-heavy small expressions could see 10-20%. Niche for the benchmark but a clean instruction-selection win for users binding ints.

Single-rounding equivalence of fild+fstp(m64) and cvtsi2sd guarantees bit-identical values.

(1) Not implemented: lines 3861-3881 still emit fild/fstp qword [rsp]/movsd for M16INT/M32INT/M64INT; lines 3850-3859 emit cvtss2sd with no dep-breaking xorps; no cvtsi2sd exists anywhere in the file. The code's own comment calls the int path "a fallback path". (2) The path is live: is_sse2_compatible (lines 3230-3277) does no type filtering, so int-typed binds compile through the SSE2 backend. (3) Bit-identical claim is correct: int16/int32 conversions are exact in both schemes; for int64, FILD is exact (64-bit significand, FILD not subject to x87 precision control) and fstp m64 rounds once under x87 RC, while cvtsi2sd r64 rounds once under MXCSR RC — identical bits under default round-to-nearest. Only divergence: user sets x87 CW rounding differently from MXCSR, an extreme edge case, and the SSE2 backend's arithmetic already follows MXCSR, so the change removes a mode inconsistency. movsx ecx matches fild word's signed semantics; RCX is volatile in both ABIs, the JIT function is nullary double(*)() (line 353), and all ECX uses in the file are in x87 transcendental blobs, not the SSE2 backend — RCX is genuinely free. cvtss2sd's upper-bit merge false dependency is real, and the xorps zero-idiom fix is standard and correctness-neutral (upper XMM bits are never observed; result read from low 64 bits of xmm0). Implementation is simpler than proposed: k_sse2_max_registers is 6 (Win)/8 (SysV) with an overflow throw, so XMM8+ never occurs and no REX.R variants are needed (the existing reg>=8 branches are dead code). (4) Side-claim verified: this is the only non-libm [rsp] use in the SSE2 backend; the minimal prologue comment (lines 5893-5895) explicitly reserves the 8-byte scratch "for int->double conversion". (5) Impact correctly self-scoped: benchmark.cpp line 489 binds only doubles, so the headline 44229-expression/6ns numbers will not change at all. Unit tests cover int16/int32/int64/float binds (unit_tests.cpp lines 405-417, 994-1017), so the change would be validated by existing tests. No NaN/-0.0/Inf concerns for integer source values. verdict.impact_assessment: Zero effect on the headline benchmark (all 44229 expressions bind doubles only) — the avg 6ns number will not move. The win is confined to users binding int16/int32/int64 (and a marginal false-dependency fix for float32 binds): per integer-variable load it replaces a 13-byte, 3-instruction x87 chain with a ~13-18 cycle store-forwarding dependency by a single 4-byte cvtsi2sd (~10 cycles including load) plus a rename-eliminated xorps. For small int-heavy expressions the claimed 10-20% eval speedup is plausible, possibly conservative. Hidden costs are negligible: +3-4 bytes per float-var load for the xorps, trivial compile-time change, and it removes the SSE2 backend's only x87 usage. A clean, low-risk instruction-selection win, but niche: real and worth doing, tiny in aggregate.

title: Omit the sub/add rsp,8 prologue/epilogue for SSE2 code that makes no calls and uses no [rsp] scratch
description: Every non-libm SSE2 function is wrapped in 'sub rsp,8' / 'add rsp,8' (5892-5896, 5905-5907), justified as scratch for int->double conversion and 16-byte alignment. But alignment only matters when the generated code itself makes calls (the libm path has its own 104-byte frame, 5887-5891), and [rsp] is only ever touched by the integer-variable conversion path (3871-3880). title: Default-on post-optimizer CSE for the SSE2 backend (dedupe surviving identical subtrees, especially repeated libm calls)

title: SSE2-native integer powers: stop pow(x, const int) from forcing the whole expression onto the x87 backend (fast_math-gated)

title: Fuse M64FP variable operands directly into SSE2 arithmetic as memory operands (addsd/subsd/mulsd/divsd xmm, [rax])

title: x87 backend: keep the RAX address cache alive across pure-FPU function blobs and re-seed it from CSE stores
description: compile_elist unconditionally sets rax_cached = nullptr after every CFUNC node (mexce.h:3149-3153), including the 2-byte pure-x87 blobs faddp/fsubp/fmulp/fdivp/fchs/fabs (Add/Sub/Mul/Div at 4710-4745, Abs at 2087) that cannot touch RAX. This forces a redundant 10-byte 'mov rax,imm64' whenever the same variable or constant address is reloaded after an intervening arithmetic op, e.g. '(x+y)*y' reloads &y immediately after the faddp. Fix: a conservative name/code whitelist (add/sub/mul/div/neg/abs and any Function whose code bytes are known pure-FPU) under which the cache is preserved; additionally, when a cse_store_suffix is appended (3146-3148) — which itself ends with 'mov rax, store_addr; fst [rax]' — set rax_cached to cse_store_addr instead of nullptr, mirroring what the SSE2 backend already does at 4084-4087. Bit-identical output; this is the same optimization PR 'Share RAX cache across compile_elist calls' (commit 4f99b9b) applied between asmd term compilations, now applied inside the walk itself.

expected_impact: Saves one 10-byte mov per avoided reload; mainly code-size/front-end. ~1-3% on affected x87 expressions, nothing on the default SSE2 path — secondary priority, but very low effort and consistent with the existing shared-RAX-cache direction of recent commits.

Verified claims (C:/plms/bsd_licensed/mexce/mexce.h):

- 4710-4743: Add/Sub/Mul/Div are exactly the 2-byte faddp/fsubp/fmulp/fdivp blobs; Neg (4746) is fchs, Abs (2087) is fabs — provably RAX-free.
- 4084-4095 (SSE2 backend): confirmed precedent — after emitting the CSE store it sets rax_cached = cse_store_addr (4087).
- 5061-5074: the x64 cse_store_suffix is exactly 'mov rax, temp_addr; fst qword ptr [rax]', and cse_store_addr is always set/copied alongside the suffix (5073-5074, 2328-2329, 2368-2369, 4509-4510, 4703-4704). - Commit 4f99b9b only shares the cache ACROSS compile_elist calls inside asmd_optimizer (4537-4541) and preserves it across the inline-emitted faddp/fchs bytes there (4584-4605); INSIDE compile_elist every CFUNC still nukes the cache. Not already implemented.

However, the headline example and part of the mechanism are wrong:
1. '(x+y)*y' never reaches this code: add/mul are SSE2-direct (3185-3194), so on x64 it compiles via the SSE2 backend, not x87.
2. More fundamentally, bare add/sub/mul/div CFUNCs essentially never survive to the x87 compile_elist: the optimizer loop (5831-5832) always runs asmd_optimizer on them, which either absorbs them into a parent (4287, node replaced by a neutral constant) or replaces them end-of-chain with fused 'add_sub_opt'/'mul_div_opt' blobs (4706) whose internal code contains its own mov rax loads and therefore legitimately clobbers the cache. 3. What IS live and would benefit: the other pure-FPU blobs that survive in x87 elists and are exactly the functions that force the x87 backend — min (2640: fcomi/fxch/fcmovb/fstp), max (2629), mod (2768: fprem), comparisons lt/le/... Patterns like min(x,y)*y or mod(x,y)+y compiled as asmd terms under the shared cache currently lose the cached &y across the pure blob and re-emit a 10-byte mov rax; a conservative whitelist correctly elides it, bit-identically (RAX in generated x87 code is used only for address materialization).

The CSE re-seed part has no such hazard.

Conclusion: I tried to refute it and failed on novelty (not implemented), correctness (bit-identical when scoped to verified-pure blobs plus the CSE re-seed), and cost (trivial). It survives as 'real', but the flagship example is invalid, the asmd-name part of the whitelist is dead, and the live benefit set is much narrower than claimed — x87-only, pattern-dependent, mostly code-size.

The concrete benefit is code size / front-end decode (10 bytes per elision, a few percent of small x87 function bodies). Worth doing only as opportunistic cleanup consistent with commit 4f99b9b; the add/sub/mul/div portion of the whitelist is dead at runtime and should be dropped from the plan.

title: Track xmm register contents and reuse repeated variable/constant values via register copies instead of memory reloads
description: compile_elist_sse2 is a pure stack machine: every CVAR occurrence re-loads from memory (mov rax,imm64 + movsd xmm,[rax]) and every non-fused CCONST re-loads from the RIP pool, even when the identical value is already sitting in an xmm register. Add a small linear-scan value tracker over the postfix walk: an array reg_content[16] recording what each xmm currently holds (variable address, constant bit pattern, or CSE-temp address). On a CVAR/CCONST load, if a register (including 'dead' registers above the current depth — e.g. xmm[d-1] still physically holds its old value after 'addsd xmm[d-2],xmm[d-1]') holds the same value, emit a reg-reg copy (movaps, see companion idea) instead of the memory load. Invalidation rules are simple and local: the destination of any arithmetic op becomes 'unknown'; after a libm call only the restored registers 0..arg_reg-1 keep their contents (the spill/restore at [rsp+48] reinstates exact bits) and everything else is invalidated; the existing CSE store (4084-4095) records reg=cse_store_addr so later cse_temp loads become free register copies — giving register-resident SSE2 CSE temps without touching run_cse. This generalizes the existing adjacent-dup peephole (3823-3836) which only catches back-to-back identical leaves. Bit-identical: a register copy yields the same 64 bits the memory load would (bound variables cannot legally change mid-evaluate; constants and CSE temps are immutable/deterministic), and constants must be matched by bit pattern (memcmp), not operator==, to preserve -0.0/NaN handling. Correctness is cheaply verifiable by bit-exact diffing evaluate() results over the 44k-expression corpus.

Worth doing, but expect single-digit low-end percent on the corpus average, verifiable cheaply by the proposed bit-exact diff.

title: Use movaps instead of merging movsd for xmm-to-xmm copies (move elimination, no false dependency)

title: Extend memory-operand fusion from constants to M64FP variables (op xmm, [rax])
description: compile_elist_sse2 already fuses a CCONST that directly precedes add/sub/mul/div into the arithmetic instruction as a RIP-relative memory operand (3895-3921 sets pending, 3928-3983 consumes it), skipping the separate load and the register slot. Do the same for M64FP CVARs: when a CVAR's next element is add/sub/mul/div, emit mov rax,addr (through the existing RAX cache) and then 'addsd/subsd/mulsd/divsd xmm[depth-1], [rax]' instead of movsd-load + reg-reg op. This is bit-identical — a scalar-sd memory operand computes exactly the same result as load-then-op. Because postfix order puts the op's RHS on top, a fused leaf is always the correct second operand, the same invariant the constant fusion relies on; and since fusion requires the next element to be the CFUNC, it can never conflict with the dup-leaf peephole (which requires the next element to be a leaf). Note normalize_commutative_operands (2929-2978) canonically places the smaller chunk (typically the lone variable) second for add/mul, so the fusable pattern is the common case. Bonus: not pushing the variable lowers live depth by one at that point, which shrinks libm spill/restore loops and reduces depth-cap pressure. Needs a second pending slot (variable address vs constant value) and new emit helpers for the [rax] operand forms (the four RIP-placeholder emitters at 3479-3545 differ only in one opcode byte; the [rax] forms are the same opcodes with ModRM 0x00+reg*8).

Risk and effort are genuinely low; strictly removes work, cannot plausibly regress eval speed.

title: On Windows, home the SSE2 value stack in callee-saved xmm6-15 for libm-bearing expressions; raise the depth cap on both ABIs
description: Two parts. (a) Bit-identical part: emit_sse2_libm_unary/binary_call currently spill every live register below the argument to [rsp+48+i*8] and reload them after every call (3707-3710, 3727-3730, 3748-3751, 3781-3784), because the stack lives in volatile xmm0-5. On Windows, xmm6-15 are callee-saved: libm must preserve them. For expressions where sse2_needs_libm_calls (3218-3227) is true, allocate stack slots starting at xmm6 (prologue saves the used xmm6..xmm(6+maxdepth-1) once with movaps into the already-reserved frame at 5887-5891, epilogue restores), keep xmm0/xmm1 only for marshalling arguments/results. Per-call spill/restore loops disappear entirely; arithmetic results are unchanged (pure register renumbering — the emitters already encode REX for reg>=8, e.g. 3367-3371, 3295-3299, 3484). (b) Behavior-changing part, to be gated (option or fast_math): raise k_sse2_max_registers (3178-3182) — trivially 8->16 on SysV where xmm8-15 are volatile and unused today, and 6->~14 on Windows with the prologue saves — so deep expressions stop failing is_sse2_compatible's depth check (3271-3273) and stop taking the x87 fallback path including its full re-parse (5843-5850). Part (b) migrates those expressions between backends, so their results match the SSE2 backend rather than current x87 output — same class of difference as the existing default SSE2-over-x87 choice, but not bit-identical to today, hence the gate.

(b) Moves deep expressions onto the faster SSE2 backend and halves their compile time by avoiding the recursive re-parse; per-expression eval gains likely 10-30% for that class

Verified xmm6-15 are never used: k_sse2_max_registers=6/8 (3178-3182) while all emitters already handle reg>=8 via REX (3367-3368, 3295-3296, 3484). NOT already implemented: k_sse2_max_registers is 6/8 (mexce.h:3178-3182), xmm6-15 are never allocated, every SSE2 libm call spills/reloads all live regs below the argument (3707-3730, 3748-3784), and the post-optimizer x87 fallback re-parses via set_expression (5843-5849). ABI claims check out: Win x64 xmm6-15 are nonvolatile (full 128 bits, so movaps saves are correctly required), libm must preserve them, and all SSE2 emitters already encode REX for reg>=8 (3367-3371, 3385-3392, 3484, cvtss2sd and CSE-store paths included) — part (a) is pure register renumbering and bit-identical; part (b) is correctly gated as value-changing (x87 80-bit/fsin vs SSE2 64-bit/libm). Measured corpus facts: cap 6 yields 43461 SSE2 / 706 x87; only 273 expressions (0.62%) emit libm calls, only 165 (0.37%) ever spill, 661 spill-pairs total — so part (a) standalone is near-noise, and 108 of the 273 libm expressions (sin(x)-style) have ZERO spills today and would be slightly regressed by homing at xmm6 keyed on the cited predicate; that predicate (sse2_needs_libm_calls, 3218-3227) also counts sqrt, which is emitted as inline sqrtsd with no call (4049-4051), so sqrt-only expressions would pay prologue saves for nothing — the gate needs refinement. Part (b) verified empirically: raising the cap to 14 migrates 425 expressions (0.96%) from x87 to SSE2 on Windows (264 for SysV 8->16), and timing exactly that migrated set gives ~190 ns/eval on x87 vs ~157 ns/eval on SSE2 (~17% faster, reproducible, within the claimed 10-30%) even without part (a)'s spill elimination. Re-parse fallbacks drop 455 -> 88, confirming the compile-time claim's effect, though its mechanism is mis-described: initially-deep expressions never re-parse (need_fallback_check is only set when the elist starts SSE2-compatible, 5659-5664); only asmd_optimizer-flattened expressions take the 5843 path. Two real implementation traps found: (1) "trivially 8->16 on SysV" is wrong — the 104-byte libm frame fits exactly 8 spill slots ([rsp+48..104)); raising the cap without growing the frame writes spills past the frame and my cap-14 build segfaulted until the prologue was grown to 184 bytes; (2) on Windows, part (b) cannot ship without part (a)'s prologue saves since depth>6 requires xmm6+. Minor costs: larger frames, a few extra movsd reg-reg marshalling moves (which have false-dependency merge semantics; movaps would be preferable), no new unwind-info exposure beyond status quo. NaN/-0.0/Inf are unaffected by register moves.
verdict.impact_assessment: Part (b) is the valuable half: ~1% of expressions migrate to SSE2, but they are the expensive tail (deep, ~190ns vs corpus avg ~6ns), measured ~17% faster per eval after migration, which works out to roughly a 4-5% reduction in aggregate corpus eval time, plus ~1% aggregate compile-time saving from eliminating ~80% of the 455 double-parse fallbacks. Part (a) standalone is essentially noise on this corpus: 0.37% of expressions spill at all (~4 spill-pairs each, around calls costing 20-100+ cycles), the prologue/epilogue movaps saves roughly cancel the win for typical shapes, and naive gating on sse2_needs_libm_calls would mildly regress no-spill sin(x)-style and sqrt-only expressions — part (a)'s real role is as the Windows enabler/complement for part (b), where migrated deep libm expressions would otherwise generate heavy spill traffic (8460 spill-pairs at cap 14 vs 661 today). Effort is medium and the claimed per-class gains are honest, but two correctness traps (frame overflow past cap 8 — empirically segfaulted — and mandatory 16-byte xmm6+ saves) make "trivial" parts of the pitch overstated.

title: SSE2 inline square-and-multiply for integer pow, ending the whole-expression x87 demotion (fast_math-gated)
description: Today any pow node anywhere in an expression demotes the entire expression to the x87 backend: 'pow' is absent from is_sse2_supported_function (3199-3208) so the pre-optimizer check (5659) clears m_sse2_simplify_mode; worse, asmd_optimizer's own SSE2-simplify reconstruction emits a pow node whenever a merged multiplicative factor exceeds 2 (4478-4482, e.g. x*x*x), and the dispatch loop skips optimizers on freshly inserted nodes, so the fallback check (5843-5850) then re-parses the whole expression from scratch with x87 forced — paying double compile cost and slower x87 eval for everything in the expression, not just the power. Fix: teach compile_elist_sse2 to emit pow(x, n) for constant integer n (|n| up to ~32, negative via one divsd from 1.0) as an SSE2 square-and-multiply using one scratch stack slot (mulsd + movaps copies, mirroring emit_integer_power_sequence's algorithm at 2165-2209), accept such pow nodes in is_sse2_compatible, and make asmd's factor>2 path use it directly. MUST be gated behind fast_math (or shipped as an explicit option): the current output computes these powers in x87 (80-bit intermediates on Linux, 53-bit-PC on Windows) so SSE2 results can differ in the last ulp — this is a backend-selection variance, not an approximation, but it is not bit-identical to current output. pow_optimizer's special-case semantics (negative bases, nested (a^b)^n folding, 2211-2373) run before codegen and are unaffected for non-integer exponents, which keep falling back as today.

evidence: Verified the chain: is_sse2_supported_function lacks pow (3185-3208); m_sse2_simplify_mode computed before optimizers (5659); asmd SSE2 mode pushes make_function(ev,"pow") for abs_factor>2 (4478-4482) and inserted nodes are skipped by the dispatch loop (insert after erase(it) at 4518-4522, loop resumes at y_next, 5786-5836); fallback then re-parses everything with prefer_x87 forced (5843-5850). x87 integer powers use 80-bit/PC-dependent fmul (2165-2209), so SSE2 mulsd output is not bit-identical -> fast_math gate required by the stated rules.

verdict.reasoning: Every cited mechanism checks out against C:\plms\bsd_licensed\mexce\mexce.h on master. (1) 'pow' is deliberately absent from is_sse2_libm_function (lines 3199-3208, with a comment explaining why) and is_sse2_compatible rejects any unsupported CFUNC (line 3255) plus any optimizer-produced function with embedded x87 code via the debug_desc check (line 3252). So a pow anywhere fails the pre-optimizer check at line 5659 and the whole expression compiles x87. (2) asmd_optimizer's SSE2-simplify reconstruction really does emit make_function(ev,"pow") whenever a merged multiplicative factor has |factor|>2 (lines 4478-4482; |factor|==2 is handled inline as x*x at 4470-4476, so only n>=3 demotes). (3) The dispatch loop captures y_next before calling the optimizer and resumes there (lines 5786-5787, 5835), and asmd inserts its reconstructed nodes via erase(it)+insert before that saved iterator (4518-4522), so the fresh pow node is never visited; even if it were, pow_optimizer would emit x87 pow_int with non-empty debug_desc, failing line 3252 anyway. Either way the fallback at 5843-5850 fires and re-parses the entire expression via set_expression with prefer_x87 forced — genuine double compile plus x87 eval for everything. (4) Not already implemented: the SSE2 backend has zero pow support of any kind; the libm-generic-pow hook (use_libm_generic_pow, mexce_libm_pow) exists only inside x87 codegen. (5) The fast_math gating is correctly scoped: the generated x87 code contains no fldcw in the prologue, so it runs at the host precision control (64-bit on Linux, 53-bit on MSVC), and SSE2 mulsd square-and-multiply is not bit-identical (last-ulp on Linux; extended-exponent-range differences near overflow/denormal even at 53-bit PC, e.g. x^-n via 1/x^n). NaN/-0.0/Inf/negative-base behavior of repeated multiplication matches the x87 reference algorithm (2165-2209) structurally. Two caveats that fall short of refutation: (a) the description claims pow_optimizer is 'unaffected', but to keep source-level x^3 on SSE2 the implementation must also stop pow_optimizer (which 'always runs', line 5829-5832) from converting integer-exponent pow into x87 pow_int in SSE2 mode, and must handle the nested (a^b)^n folding that depends on m_power_terms populated by that path (corpus contains e.g. "a^2^3") — real added effort, consistent with the stated 'medium' rating; (b) the 'compile time roughly halves' claim only applies to the asmd-emitted-pow fallback case — source-^ expressions fail the pre-check before optimizers run and never double-compile today, so they gain eval speed only.

Verified corpus counts: exactly 170/44229 (0.38%) expressions contain '^'; of those ~104 have constant integer-looking exponents (66 are a^b or non-integer, which the fix does not help and which keep falling back), and several are pure-constant and fold away entirely — so the genuinely targeted set is roughly 0.2% of the corpus. Expected aggregate benchmark movement: well under 0.1% on both eval and compile averages. Per affected expression the 20-50% eval gain from staying on SSE2 is plausible but unmeasured (the x87 pow_int path is itself just a few fmuls; the gain comes from avoiding the x87 backend for the rest of the expression). The stronger justification is real user code (polynomial kernels, x^2+y^2-style distance math), where integer powers are far more common than in this corpus — but that is outside the measured benchmark.

title: x87: stop invalidating the RAX address cache after pure-FPU function blobs in compile_elist
description: compile_elist unconditionally invalidates its RAX cache after every CFUNC node (rax_cached = nullptr at 3149-3153), but the most common inline blobs cannot touch RAX: add/sub/mul/div are 2-byte faddp/fsubp/fmulp/fdivp (4710-4743), neg is fchs (4749-4751), min/max are fcomi/fcmovb/fxch/fstp (2629-2649), abs is fabs, sqrt is fsqrt; floor/ceil touch only RSP. Add a 'clobbers_rax' flag to Function (default true, set false for these prototypes) and skip invalidation accordingly. This directly extends commit 4f99b9b's shared-RAX-cache work: that commit preserved the cache *between* asmd term compilations, but each compile_elist call still self-invalidates internally, so a term chunk like '(x+1)*(x+2)' re-emits the 10-byte 'mov rax,&x' after the first faddp even though RAX still holds &x. Bit-identical by construction — only redundant mov rax,imm64 instructions are removed; the loaded values and all FPU computation are untouched. Benefits the x87 backend, which on x64 still serves all expressions with comparisons (lt/gt/le/ge/eq/ne), min/max/mod/sign/gain/bias, pow-optimized blobs, deep expressions, and all 32-bit builds... note on 32-bit the cache doesn't exist (moffs addressing), so this is x64-x87 only.

Invalidate the cache') and that Add/Sub/Mul/Div/Neg are 2-byte pure-FPU sequences (DE C1 / DE E9 / DE C9 / DE F9 / D9 E0 at 4712-4751), Min/Max use only FPU opcodes (2631-2648). The core mechanism is sound: the cited blobs are genuinely RAX-pure (Neg D9E0, Abs D9E1, Sqrt D9FA, Min/Max fcomi/fcmov/fxch/fstp at 2629-2649, Mod fxch/fprem/fstp, lt/le/gt/ge/eq/ne fcomip/fld1/fldz/fcmov/fstp at 2779-2857, Floor/Ceil RSP-only), and eliding a redundant mov rax,imm64 when RAX provably holds the same address is bit-identical. However, three substantive flaws: (1) As specified it is NOT bit-identical — the CSE store suffix emitted right after function code (3146-3147) is 'mov rax,temp_addr; fst [rax]' on x64 (5062-5065), so skipping invalidation for a pure-flagged CSE source (e.g. shared sqrt under enable_cse) leaves a stale cache and produces wrong results; the skip must also require cse_store_suffix.empty() (or set rax_cached=cse_store_addr). Trivially fixable, but the 'bit-identical by construction' claim is false as written. (2) The flagship targets add/sub/mul/div (4710-4743) are dead code for runtime: the optimizer loop (5786-5836) runs asmd_optimizer unconditionally (not fast_math-gated), so in the x87 path these nodes are always absorbed or replaced by add_sub_opt/mul_div_opt blobs; raw faddp blobs reach compile_elist only during compile-time constant folding (5815-5819). (3) The headline example '(x+1)*(x+2)' is invalid twice over: it is SSE2-compatible (default x64 path, no RAX cache), and even under prefer_x87 each inner add becomes a separately pre-compiled add_sub_opt blob (fresh rax_cache at 4540) whose redundant 'mov rax,&x' is baked into Function::code, unreachable by the flag. Within that class, only expressions that reload the currently-cached address immediately after a pure-FPU op benefit, saving one 10-byte mov rax,imm64 each (typically 1-2 per expression, and only in some term-sort orderings). A mov rax,imm64 is ~0.25 cycles throughput and sits off the FPU dependency chain; in code dominated by fsqrt/fcomip/fprem/transcendentals (tens to hundreds of cycles) it is almost fully hidden by out-of-order execution. The dependable benefits are JIT code size (10 bytes per elision, mild icache help when many expressions are hot) and negligible compile-time savings. Effort is genuinely small and consistent with the merged 4f99b9b micro-optimization, so it is a reasonable cleanup, but expect code-size wins rather than measurable speedup.
